title: Lead time
text:
Lead time
Definition: Lead time is the time between placing a replenishment order (or shipping an order) and receiving the goods.
Why it matters: Longer or more variable lead times force a planner to hold more stock during the replenishment window, so lead time directly drives reorder points and safety stock.
Formula: Lead-time demand = average daily demand x lead time in days.
Example: With 20 units of daily demand and a 5-day lead time, lead-time demand is 100 units.

title: Safety stock
text:
Safety stock
Definition: Safety stock is extra inventory held to protect against demand or lead-time variability during replenishment.
Why it matters: It is the buffer that keeps the stockout probability at the chosen service level; too little causes lost sales, too much ties up cash.
Formula: Safety stock = z x standard deviation of demand per day x square root of lead time in days.
Example: For a 95% service level (z = 1.65), daily demand standard deviation 8 and a 9-day lead time: 1.65 x 8 x 3 = 39.6, about 40 units.

title: Reorder point
text:
Reorder point
Definition: Reorder point is the inventory level at which a new replenishment order should be placed.
Why it matters: Ordering at the right level means stock arrives just before it runs out; ordering late causes stockouts and ordering early inflates inventory.
Formula: Reorder point = average daily demand x lead time + safety stock.
Example: With 20 units/day, a 5-day lead time and 30 units of safety stock, the reorder point is 130 units.

title: Economic order quantity (EOQ)
text:
Economic order quantity (EOQ)
Definition: Economic order quantity (EOQ) is the order size that minimises the sum of ordering cost and holding cost.
Why it matters: It balances many small expensive orders against few large orders that raise holding cost.
Formula: EOQ = square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order / annual holding cost per unit).
Example: Annual demand 12,000, ordering cost 50, holding cost 4 per unit per year: sqrt(2 x 12000 x 50 / 4) = about 548 units.

title: Service level
text:
Service level
Definition: Service level is the target probability of not stocking out during a replenishment cycle.
Why it matters: It sets the z-value used in the safety-stock formula; a higher service level needs disproportionately more safety stock.
Formula: Common z-values: 90% = 1.28, 95% = 1.65, 97.5% = 1.96, 99% = 2.33.

title: Fill rate
text:
Fill rate
Definition: Fill rate is the share of demand that is met immediately from stock.
Why it matters: It measures how much demand was actually satisfied, and can differ from cycle service level because it counts units rather than cycles.
Formula: Fill rate = units shipped from stock / units demanded.

title: Stockout
text:
Stockout
Definition: Stockout is a situation where demand occurs but no inventory is available to serve it.
Why it matters: Stockouts cause lost sales, backorders and unhappy customers, and are the main cost that safety stock is designed to prevent.

title: Backorder
text:
Backorder
Definition: Backorder is customer demand that could not be filled immediately and is fulfilled later when stock arrives.
Why it matters: Backorders keep the sale but hurt delivery performance and raise late-delivery rates.

title: Cycle stock
text:
Cycle stock
Definition: Cycle stock is the part of inventory that is used up between replenishments under normal conditions.
Why it matters: It is driven by order size, so larger EOQ-type orders increase average cycle stock.
Formula: Average cycle stock = order quantity / 2.
Example: An order quantity of 480 units gives an average cycle stock of 240 units.

title: Holding cost
text:
Holding cost
Definition: Holding cost is the yearly cost of keeping inventory, including capital, storage, insurance and obsolescence.
Why it matters: It is the force that pushes order sizes down in EOQ; it is often estimated as a percentage of unit price.
Formula: Annual holding cost per unit = holding rate x unit price.
Example: A 20% holding rate on a $50 item gives $10 per unit per year.

title: Ordering cost
text:
Ordering cost
Definition: Ordering cost is the fixed cost of placing and receiving one replenishment order, regardless of its size.
Why it matters: High ordering cost pushes toward larger, less frequent orders.

title: Inventory turnover
text:
Inventory turnover
Definition: Inventory turnover is how many times inventory is sold and replaced during a period.
Why it matters: Low turnover means capital is stuck in slow-moving stock; very high turnover can signal stockout risk.
Formula: Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory value.
Example: COGS of 1,200,000 with average inventory of 200,000 gives a turnover of 6 times per year.

title: Days of supply
text:
Days of supply
Definition: Days of supply is how many days the current stock will last at the current demand rate.
Why it matters: It converts an inventory count into a time buffer that planners can compare to lead time.
Formula: Days of supply = inventory on hand / average daily demand.
Example: 300 units on hand with 20 units/day demand is 15 days of supply.

title: ABC analysis
text:
ABC analysis
Definition: ABC analysis is a classification of items by their share of total value, so that attention goes to the items that matter most.
Why it matters: Class A items (roughly the top 70% of value) get tight control and frequent review, B items moderate control and C items simple rules.
Formula: Sort items by value, compute cumulative share; A = first ~70%, B = next ~20%, C = last ~10%.

title: Demand forecasting
text:
Demand forecasting
Definition: Demand forecasting is estimating future demand from historical data and other signals.
Why it matters: Forecasts feed reorder points, safety stock and purchasing; forecast error is what safety stock has to absorb.

title: Forecast error
text:
Forecast error
Definition: Forecast error is the gap between actual demand and the forecast, commonly summarised as MAE, RMSE or MAPE.
Why it matters: The standard deviation of forecast error is the right variability input for safety stock, because that is the uncertainty left after forecasting.
Formula: MAE = mean(|actual - forecast|); RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - forecast)^2)); MAPE = mean(|actual - forecast| / actual) x 100.
Example: Forecasts of 90 and 110 against actuals of 100 and 100 give MAE 10, RMSE 10 and MAPE 10%.

title: Exponential smoothing
text:
Exponential smoothing
Definition: Exponential smoothing is a forecasting method that weights recent observations more heavily using a smoothing parameter alpha.
Why it matters: It reacts to level changes while smoothing noise, and needs only a short history, which suits many products.
Formula: Level_t = alpha x actual_t + (1 - alpha) x Level_(t-1); next forecast = latest level.

title: Moving average
text:
Moving average
Definition: Moving average is a forecast equal to the average of the most recent n periods.
Why it matters: It is a simple, robust baseline that works with very short histories but lags behind trends.
Formula: 3-month moving average forecast = (D_t + D_(t-1) + D_(t-2)) / 3.
Example: Demand of 100, 110 and 120 gives a forecast of 110.

title: Bullwhip effect
text:
Bullwhip effect
Definition: Bullwhip effect is the amplification of demand variability as orders move upstream from retailer to supplier.
Why it matters: It leads to excess inventory and capacity swings upstream; sharing demand data and shorter lead times reduce it.

title: Just-in-time
text:
Just-in-time
Definition: Just-in-time is a replenishment approach that delivers materials only when needed, minimising inventory.
Why it matters: It cuts holding cost but leaves little buffer, so it depends on reliable lead times.

title: Lead-time variability
text:
Lead-time variability
Definition: Lead-time variability is the fluctuation of actual lead times around their average.
Why it matters: Unreliable lead times require extra safety stock; reducing variability is often cheaper than holding buffer inventory.

title: Late delivery risk
text:
Late delivery risk
Definition: Late delivery risk is the probability that an order is delivered later than its scheduled shipping window.
Why it matters: It lets planners intervene early on risky orders, for example by expediting or switching the shipping mode.
Formula: In the DataCo data an order item counts as late when actual shipping days exceed scheduled shipping days.

title: Shipping mode
text:
Shipping mode
Definition: Shipping mode is the delivery service level chosen for an order: Standard Class (4 scheduled days), Second Class (2), First Class (1) or Same Day (0).
Why it matters: The scheduled window is very short for premium modes, so they are missed more often; in the DataCo data First Class has the highest late rate and Standard Class the lowest.

title: Shipping delay
text:
Shipping delay
Definition: Shipping delay is actual shipping days minus scheduled shipping days, where scheduled days are the promised window and actual days are what happened.
Why it matters: A positive delay means the order was late, but it is only known after shipment, so it cannot be used as a feature to predict lateness in advance.
Formula: Shipping delay = actual shipping days - scheduled shipping days.
Example: Scheduled 2 days and actual 5 days gives a delay of 3 days.

title: Coefficient of variation
text:
Coefficient of variation
Definition: Coefficient of variation is the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, a scale-free measure of variability.
Why it matters: It makes variability comparable across products with very different volumes and is used here to rate forecast risk.
Formula: CV = standard deviation / mean.
Example: A standard deviation of 20 on a mean of 100 gives a CV of 0.20.

title: (s, Q) reorder policy
text:
(s, Q) reorder policy
Definition: (s, Q) reorder policy is a continuous-review policy that orders a fixed quantity Q whenever inventory position falls to the reorder point s.
Why it matters: It pairs naturally with EOQ for Q and the reorder-point formula for s.

title: Data leakage
text:
Data leakage
Definition: Data leakage is using information in a model that would not be available at prediction time.
Why it matters: For late-delivery prediction, features such as delivery status, actual shipping days or shipping delay reveal the outcome, so they must be excluded or the model looks unrealistically accurate.

title: ROC-AUC
text:
ROC-AUC
Definition: ROC-AUC is the probability that a model ranks a random positive case above a random negative case, summarising ranking quality across thresholds.
Why it matters: It is threshold-free, so it compares classifiers fairly; 0.5 is random and 1.0 is perfect.

title: Cycle service level
text:
Cycle service level
Definition: Cycle service level is the probability of having no stockout in a replenishment cycle, which differs from fill rate, the fraction of units served.
Why it matters: Two policies with the same cycle service level can have different fill rates, so always state which measure a target refers to.

title: Late-delivery prediction model
text:
Late-delivery prediction model
An XGBoost classifier predicts whether an order item will be late using five features known at order time: Shipping Mode, Days for shipment (scheduled), Type, Customer Segment, Order Region. It is trained on the past and tested on the most recent orders (9,026 test rows). Test ROC-AUC 0.7397, accuracy 0.6959, precision 0.8342, recall 0.5577. Post-outcome columns (delivery status, actual shipping days, shipping delay) are excluded to avoid data leakage.

title: Inventory policy assumptions
text:
Inventory policy assumptions
Service level 95% (z = 1.65); ordering cost $50 per order; holding cost 20% of unit price per year. The dataset contains outbound shipping days, not supplier lead times, so each product's average shipping days (minimum 1 day) is used as its replenishment lead time. Safety stock = z x forecast-error standard deviation x sqrt(lead time in months). Reorder point = monthly forecast x lead time in months + safety stock. Products with too little history use the pooled coefficient of variation of well-forecast products, and are marked with lower data confidence.
